name: a(n) = is the smallest m >= 1 such that n! = b_1*...*b_t with b_1 < ... < b_t and m = b_t - b_1.
comment: Empirical observation: while generating this sequence, it seems like searching for factors around a window of (n!)^(1/k), where 2 <= k <= n will find likely matches. This is due to the geometric mean of k factors being near (n!)^(1/k). No proof if this heuristic method guarantees finding valid factors, or a numerical lower bound on the window width.
When m = 0 is allowed we would have a(n) = 0 for all n and we could define a(1).
As m >= 1, t > 1 and so b_1*b_t <= n! and so b_1 < sqrt(n!) (< as for n >= 2 we have n! is never a square).
a(n) <= min(A061057(n), n-2) for n>=3 where upper bound n-2 comes from t = n-1, b_1 = 2, b_t = n. (End)
reference: P. Erdős and R. Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980), p. 76.
